title: Dataset Loading
content:
Users can keep task inputs and metadata in the same dataset, with a separate split for evaluation. This guide prepares training and evaluation data for the length-ratio task from the quick start.
Dataset Splits# Each dataset row is a dictionary. The default formatter reads its prompt field; additional fields can hold targets, labels, test cases, or other information required by the reward function. Trainers pass the original row to the reward function through batch_items.
from datasets import Dataset dataset = Dataset.from_dict({ "prompt": [ "Describe a city in the clouds.", "Invent a new holiday.", "Write a bedtime story for a dragon.", "Explain how teleportation might work.", "Tell a story about dinosaurs.", "Describe a world without electricity.", "Create a superhero with a unique power.", "Write a scene where the moon talks.", "Invent a new type of fruit.", "Design a playground on Mars.", ], "target_min": [2.0] * 10, "target_max": [3.0] * 10, }) split = dataset.train_test_split(test_size=0.2, seed=42) train_dataset = split["train"] eval_dataset = split["test"]Here, eight rows are used for training and two are held out for evaluation. seed makes the split repeatable; it does not set the random seed for model generation. Existing training and validation splits can be used directly.
The current training data loaders preserve dataset order. Users can shuffle the data with train_dataset.shuffle(seed=42) before creating the trainer. This produces a fixed order, without reshuffling each epoch.
Prompts and Rewards# Users can share a prompt format across agents with one formatter, or assign different roles with a list of formatters in actor order. Only fields used by the formatter enter the model prompt; the reward function can still read the full row.
import math def brief_formatter(item): return f"Write a short response to this task:\n{item['prompt']}" def detailed_formatter(item): return f"Write a detailed response to this task:\n{item['prompt']}" formatters = [brief_formatter, detailed_formatter] def reward_func(brief_completions, detailed_completions, *, batch_items): item = batch_items[0] rewards = [] for brief, detailed in zip(brief_completions, detailed_completions): if not brief: rewards.append(0.0) continue ratio = len(detailed) / len(brief) distance = max(item["target_min"] - ratio, ratio - item["target_max"], 0.0) rewards.append(math.exp(-distance)) return rewardsEach completion argument is a list of strings for one agent. The trainers used here call the reward function for one dataset row at a time, with that row available as batch_items[0]. This function returns one shared reward per aligned pair of responses. The task rewards a character-count ratio; it does not measure writing quality, and the agents generate independently.
Users can check the data and reward function without loading models:
item = train_dataset[0] assert item["prompt"] in brief_formatter(item) assert reward_func(["Hi"], ["Hello"], batch_items=[item]) == [1.0] assert reward_func([""], ["Hello"], batch_items=[item]) == [0.0]For multi-turn tasks, formatters may also accept external_prompts. The transition interface is described in Multi-Turn Interaction.
Training and Evaluation# Users can provide training and evaluation data separately through train_dataset and eval_dataset. Evaluation uses the training formatters and reward function without updating model weights. Outputs are sampled with the configured generation settings, so repeated evaluations can produce different scores.
from comlrl.trainers.reinforce import MAGRPOConfig, MAGRPOTrainer config = MAGRPOConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, num_train_epochs=1, num_generations=4, max_new_tokens=128, eval_interval=4, eval_num_samples=len(eval_dataset), eval_batch_size=1, logging_steps=4, ) trainer = MAGRPOTrainer( agent_model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B", num_agents=2, formatters=formatters, reward_func=reward_func, train_dataset=train_dataset, eval_dataset=eval_dataset, args=config, ) trainer.train() metrics = trainer.evaluate(num_eval_samples=len(eval_dataset)) print(metrics)For the MAREINFORCE family, IAC, and MAAC, eval_interval counts training dataset items. Evaluation runs before item zero of each epoch, then at the configured interval; 0 enables manual evaluation only. eval_num_samples specifies a positive limit on evaluated rows, starting at the beginning of the evaluation split. Setting it to the split length evaluates all rows. eval_batch_size controls the evaluation data loader batch size, not the number of responses generated per agent.
MAGRPO, IAC, and MAAC generate one response per agent per turn during evaluation. IAC and MAAC use their rollout collection path, with the configured turn structure, but their evaluate() method takes no sample-count argument:
# For an existing IACTrainer or MAACTrainer: ac_trainer.args.eval_num_samples = len(eval_dataset) metrics = ac_trainer.evaluate()Without an eval_dataset, evaluate() returns an empty dictionary. For MAPL, manual evaluate(num_eval_samples=...) is also available; the automatic evaluation schedule follows the preference-update or actor-training stage rather than the dataset-item schedule above.
Logging Metric covers saving evaluation results, recording training curves, and adding custom metrics.

title: Multi-Agent DPO
content:
Multi-Agent Direct Preference Optimization (MADPO) trains the agents directly from preferred and rejected joint responses, without a reward model or a separate RL stage. Its loss combines all agents’ preference margins, so each policy learns from the team’s outcome.
The training flow is: task items → preference pairs → joint preference loss → policy updates. MARLHF uses the same pairs to fit a joint reward model first and then trains the policies with RL.
The diagram uses the same task item and preference pairs as the MARLHF figure; here the agents’ margins enter one joint loss directly.
MADPO training flow The agents' margins on each preference pair add up to one joint loss that updates every policy directly. Pairs Policy scores Joint loss UpdateEach agent Per agent No reward model Complete diagram Play Replay Preference Pairs# Each agent \( i\in\mathcal{I}=\{1,\ldots,n\} \) samples \( a_{i,t}\sim\pi_{\theta_i}(\cdot\mid h_{i,t}) \) from its local history; the responses form the joint action \( \mathbf{a}_t=\{a_{1,t},\ldots,a_{n,t}\} \) with joint history \( \mathbf{h}_t \). Only a single turn is currently supported (horizon \( H=1 \)), so \( h_{i,0} \) is agent \( i \)’s prompt and \( \mathbf{a}_0 \) is the joint response.
For each task item in train_dataset, every agent samples preference_num_candidates responses from its formatted prompt. Responses with the same candidate index form a joint response and share one reward from reward_func (after the optional reward_processor). For two joint responses with different rewards, the response with the higher reward is the winner \( w \) and the other the loser \( l \); ties are discarded. Each pair \( (\mathbf{h}_H^{w},\mathbf{h}_H^{l}) \) contains the two joint histories for one task.
The base trainer collects the pairs once and reuses them for num_train_epochs; pair_selection and preference_pairs_per_sample determine which pairs are retained for each task.
MADPO currently requires num_turns=1 and joint_mode="aligned". pair_selection="all" requires preference_pairs_per_sample=None. If no task yields a non-tied pair, training returns without updating the policies.
Joint Preference Objective# Each agent’s margin is the difference between its log-probabilities for the winning and losing responses. The joint margin sums these differences across agents:
\[ \Delta_{\theta_i}=\sum_{t=0}^{H-1}\Big(\log\pi_{\theta_i}(a_{i,t}^{w}\mid h_{i,t}^{w})-\log\pi_{\theta_i}(a_{i,t}^{l}\mid h_{i,t}^{l})\Big), \qquad \Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}}\Delta_{\theta_i}. \] MADPO minimizes
\[ \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MADPO}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =-\mathbb{E}_{(\mathbf{h}_H^{w},\mathbf{h}_H^{l})\sim\mathcal{B}} \Big[\log\sigma\big(\eta\,\Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\big)\Big], \] where \( \sigma \) is the sigmoid function, \( \eta>0 \) is dpo_beta (default 0.1), and \( \mathcal{B} \) is the set of training pairs. The task reward determines only the ordering within each pair; the loss itself uses the policies’ log-probabilities.
The gradient for agent \( i \) is
\[ \nabla_{\theta_i}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{MADPO}}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) =-\eta\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{B}} \Big[\sigma\big(-\eta\,\Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}\big)\,\nabla_{\theta_i}\Delta_{\theta_i}\Big]. \] The weight \( \sigma(-\eta\,\Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}) \) depends on the team’s joint margin, while the gradient flows only through agent \( i \)’s own margin. In each batch, the trainer computes all margins once without gradients, then updates each agent with its own differentiable margin plus the others’ detached margins.
Reference-Free Implementation# Equation 6 of the MAPL paper replaces \( \log\pi_{\theta_i} \) in \( \Delta_{\theta_i} \) with the log-ratio \( \log(\pi_{\theta_i}/\pi_{\mathrm{ref},i}) \) against a frozen reference policy. CoMLRL implements the reference-free form above: the inherited reference_kl_enabled, reference_kl_coef, and reference_devices settings do not add reference terms to the MADPO loss.
The decentralized scorer excludes the last completion token after trimming padding, so each agent’s margin omits that token’s log-probability. The centralized scorer covers the full joint completion.
Configuration# Users can import MADPOConfig and MADPOTrainer from comlrl.trainers.preference.
MADPOConfig Parameters num_agents: Number of agents in decentralized mode, or task roles in centralized mode collaboration_mode: "decentralized" (default) or "centralized" num_train_epochs: Optimization epochs over the collected preference pairs agent_learning_rate: Policy learning rate preference_num_candidates: Candidates sampled per task and actor; at least 2 preference_pairs_per_sample: Maximum pairs retained per task, or None for no limit pair_selection: "reward_gap" selects pairs with the largest reward gaps, "random" selects a random subset, and "all" retains every non-tied pair dpo_beta: Positive coefficient on the joint margin train_batch_size: Preference pairs per update; defaults to rollout_buffer_size max_new_tokens, temperature, top_p, top_k: Candidate generation settings parallel_training, agent_devices: Policy execution mode and device placement eval_interval, eval_num_samples, eval_batch_size: Evaluation schedule and sample sizes; MADPO counts eval_interval in preference updates logging_steps: Training logging interval MADPOTrainer Parameters agent_model or agents: Model identifier for homogeneous agents, or a list of model identifiers or instances num_agents: Number of agents or task roles; must match args.num_agents tokenizer: One tokenizer, or one per actor train_dataset: Task items from which preference candidates are generated eval_dataset: Optional evaluation dataset reward_func: Required callable returning one shared reward per aligned joint response reward_processor: Optional post-processing of task rewards formatters: One prompt formatter shared by all roles, or a list of role-specific formatters args: MADPOConfig instance model_config: Optional model loading configuration wandb_config: Optional Weights & Biases configuration eval_logger, eval_aggregator: Optional evaluation metrics hooks, as in MAGRPOTrainer centralized_comparator_adapter: Prompt builder and response parser for centralized actors or comparators Evaluation samples responses from the current policies and scores them with the task reward. The training metrics turn_1/reward_mean and turn_1/expected_return instead average the candidate rewards recorded when the pairs were collected; they do not reflect the updated policies.
Collaboration and Iterative Training# Decentralized MADPO trains one policy per agent with the summed margin \( \Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \). With collaboration_mode="centralized", one actor \( \boldsymbol{\pi}_{\boldsymbol{\theta}}(\mathbf{a}_t\mid\mathbf{h}_t) \) generates the complete joint response, and \( \Delta_{\boldsymbol{\theta}} \) is that actor’s margin on the joint text. num_agents must equal the number of task roles, and the configuration requires one actor and tokenizer. The joint text is retained for preference training and parsed into role responses only for task rewards and evaluation. Training Framework describes the layouts and adapter interface.
MADPOIterTrainer repeats data collection and training. Iteration \( \nu \) pairs each new current-policy sample with the comparator sample at the same candidate index (either side can win), then applies the MADPO updates to the selected pairs \( \mathcal{B}^{(\nu)} \). An iteration is not a dialog turn, so the single-turn, aligned-response restriction still applies.
Training Framework describes the iterative configuration, the comparator, and the replay buffer that selects \( \mathcal{B}^{(\nu)} \).

title: Multi-LLM PbRL
content:
Multi-Agent Preference Learning (MAPL) improves collaborating agents by comparing joint responses to the same task. A preference identifies a better and a worse joint response, so each agent learns in the context of the team’s outcome.
CoMLRL provides two approaches: MADPO directly optimizes the policies from preference pairs, while MARLHF first learns a joint reward model and then trains the policies with that reward. Their iterative variants refresh the preference data as training progresses. MAPL names this family of methods; the public trainer classes are MADPOTrainer, MARLHFTrainer, MADPOIterTrainer, and MARLHFIterTrainer.
The following pages cover the shared training framework and the two learning approaches:
Training Framework: Actor and comparator layouts, iterative training, comparator sources, and replay. MARLHF: Two-stage learning with a joint reward model followed by policy optimization. MADPO: Direct policy optimization from joint preference pairs. Preference Pairs# For a task with per-agent prompts \( \mathbf{h}=(h_1,\ldots,h_N) \), the trainer samples candidate joint responses \( \mathbf{a}^{k}=(a_1^k,\ldots,a_N^k) \). Candidates with the same index are aligned across agents and receive a shared scalar task reward. A pair is ordered as \( \mathbf{a}^{+}\succ\mathbf{a}^{-} \) when the first response has a strictly higher reward. Ties are discarded.
The training dataset contains task items used to construct prompts. By default, the formatter reads each item’s prompt field; custom formatters can use other fields or provide different prompts for each role. The trainers generate and score their own preference pairs from these items. The base MADPO and MARLHF trainers collect those pairs once before optimization.
All four preference trainers currently require num_turns=1 and aligned joint responses (joint_mode="aligned"). The iterative variants repeat data collection and training; an iteration is not a dialog turn.
MARLHF# Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback first fits a joint reward model to preferred and rejected team responses, then optimizes the policies with the learned reward. The MARLHF page describes the reward objective and policy-training workflow.
The MARLHFConfig parameters and MARLHFTrainer setup are documented on that page.
MADPO# Multi-Agent Direct Preference Optimization updates the policies directly from preferred and rejected joint responses. The MADPO page describes its joint preference loss and training workflow.
The MADPOConfig parameters and MADPOTrainer setup are documented on that page.
Iterative Training# MADPOIterTrainer and MARLHFIterTrainer alternate preference collection with optimization. Training Framework describes the training cycle, the comparator, and the replay buffer.
Collaboration Modes# Preference training supports separate policies per role or one actor generating the complete joint response. Training Framework describes the supported actor/comparator layouts and centralized adapters.

title: Logging Metric
content:
CoMLRL supports local evaluation records, training curves in Weights & Biases, and task-specific metrics. The examples use the trainer and held-out split from Dataset Loading.
Local Metrics# Evaluation returns a metrics dictionary even when W&B is disabled. Users can save this dictionary locally to record a completed evaluation:
import json from pathlib import Path # Use the MAGRPO trainer and eval_dataset from the Dataset Loading guide. metrics = trainer.evaluate(num_eval_samples=len(eval_dataset)) Path("eval-metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(metrics, indent=2) + "\n")Weights & Biases# Users can record training curves in Weights & Biases by supplying wandb_config when creating the trainer:
wandb_config = { "project": "comlrl", "name": "length-ratio-magrpo", "tags": ["length-ratio", "magrpo"], "config_sections": { "dataset": {"name": "length-ratio", "split_seed": 42}, "output": {"verbose": True}, }, } # Add this keyword when constructing MAGRPOTrainer: # wandb_config=wandb_config,Users can authenticate W&B in their environment before enabling logging. Omitting wandb_config or setting it to None disables W&B. Supported run settings include project, entity, name (or run_name), tags, and dir. The config_sections field adds dataset and experiment settings to the recorded configuration; config_sections.output.verbose controls trainer progress output.
Training Metrics# MARL trainers log against env_step, the count of joint-action reward evaluations. This differs from the dataset index or optimizer-update count, especially with multiple generations or turns. Standard training metrics are logged when rollout buffers are processed, with logging_steps specifying the minimum env_step gap between logs. Evaluation follows eval_interval independently.
Metric Meaning turn_1/reward_mean Mean immediate reward in the logged training rollouts at turn 1 turn_1/expected_return Mean return stored for those training rollouts eval/turn_1/reward_mean Mean immediate reward in evaluation rollouts at turn 1 eval/turn_1/expected_return Mean evaluation return from turn 1 Turn numbers start at 1. MAGRPO evaluation returns are undiscounted sums of rewards from the current turn onward; IAC and MAAC report their collected rollout returns. Rewards reflect the configured reward processing, and actor-critic returns can also include reference-KL shaping when enabled. The single-turn example in Dataset Loading uses the default identity reward processor and no reference KL, so its reward and return metrics describe the same task score.
Custom Metrics# Users can add custom evaluation metrics to MAGRPO by supplying an eval_logger and an eval_aggregator together. The logger receives completions in [agent][dataset item][turn] order plus the original batch_items and raw prompts. The aggregator returns scalar metrics without the eval/ prefix; the trainer adds it.
The following example measures the average response length across agents at each turn:
def eval_logger(*, agent_completions_turns, batch_items, prompts): return [ { f"turn_{turn + 1}/response_chars": sum( len(agent[row][turn]) for agent in agent_completions_turns ) / len(agent_completions_turns) for turn in range(len(agent_completions_turns[0][row])) } for row in range(len(batch_items)) ] def eval_aggregator(rows, *, num_turns): return { key: sum(row[key] for row in rows) / len(rows) for turn in range(num_turns) for key in [f"turn_{turn + 1}/response_chars"] } if rows else {} # Add both keywords when constructing MAGRPOTrainer: # eval_logger=eval_logger, # eval_aggregator=eval_aggregator,The resulting dictionary includes eval/turn_1/response_chars. These callbacks also receive metadata fields, allowing task-specific accuracy or group metrics to be computed without reference answers in the prompts.
IAC and MAAC instead accept metrics_callback(rollouts), which returns a dictionary of numeric values. Each rollout sample provides fields such as agent_idx, prompt, completion, and metadata:
def metrics_callback(rollouts): if not rollouts: return {} return { "response_chars": sum(len(sample.completion) for sample in rollouts) / len(rollouts) } # Add metrics_callback=metrics_callback to IACTrainer(...) or MAACTrainer(...).This callback runs during both training and evaluation. Evaluation averages its values across evaluated dataset items and adds eval/; training logs its values at rollout collection time, separately from the standard logging_steps gate.

title: Training Parallelization
content:
CoMLRL trainers run in a Python process. For IAC, parallel_training="none" is the default; "mp" enables scheduling agents and critics on explicitly assigned devices. Neither mode requires a job scheduler.
Model Parallelization# Users can configure IACTrainer by passing an IACConfig through its args parameter. The following configuration uses four visible CUDA devices and two agents:
from comlrl.trainers.actor_critic import IACConfig config = IACConfig( num_agents=2, num_turns=1, use_separate_critic=True, parallel_training="mp", agent_devices=["cuda:0", "cuda:1"], critic_devices=["cuda:2", "cuda:3"], )agent_devices is required in "mp" mode. critic_devices is also required when use_separate_critic=True. Each model stays on its assigned device; this does not split an individual model across GPUs. Responses are passed to the reward function, and the rewards are used for each agent’s update.
Device indices refer to the GPUs visible to the Python process. Users can choose device assignments based on the available devices and each model’s memory requirements. Device placement and parallel scheduling can affect numerical training results.

title: Q&A
content:
What are the differences between CoMLRL and other multi-LLM training frameworks? Many approaches train role-conditioned agents with shared parameters using single-agent RL frameworks. Distinct agents better represent heterogeneous LLMs with different capabilities and more directly reflect the multi-agent setting.
CoMLRL supports separate actors with decentralized execution, including training with a centralized critic. Its centralized collaboration mode instead uses one actor to generate the complete joint response. The available trainers include REINFORCE, Actor-Critic, and Multi-Agent Preference Learning; each method’s page describes its implemented objective and constraints.
Does CoMLRL support single-agent fine-tuning? Yes. Users can set num_agents=1 for single-agent fine-tuning. CoMLRL prioritizes simple multi-agent training and omits some optimizations, so its single-agent trainers may not be optimal. LLaMA-Factory, trl, OpenRLHF, and verl are alternatives for single-agent fine-tuning.
Does CoMLRL support self-play/self-improvement/self-evolution with MARL? Yes. Although CoMLRL focuses on LLM collaboration formalized as a Dec-POMDP, users can customize environment interactions to implement pipelines such as self-play (Spiral) and self-improvement (MAFT). The multi-turn training documentation provides further details.
Does CoMLRL support distributed training? CoMLRL supports assigning whole actor and critic models to multiple devices with parallel_training="mp" in one Python process. It does not provide multi-process data-parallel training or shard an individual model across devices. Training Parallelization describes device configuration.
